items.title: Bellman Meets Lyapunov: Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning via Mastering Chaos
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a powerful paradigm for training agents, yet its success rests on domain expertise of human engineers who design informative reward signals for every new task. Unsupervised RL aims to reduce this engineering with intrinsic motivation (IM): reward signals that emerge from the agent environment interaction itself. Existing IM objectives, however, involve the selection of information variables, which re-introduces domain expertise the field has sought to eliminate. We introduce Forward CIP (F-CIP), an RL-native formulation of the Controllable Information Production (CIP) objective, which is defined by the system's dynamics alone and requires no such selection. We prove that F-CIP is compatible with RL and demonstrate its effectiveness with existing algorithms. Training agents with F-CIP results in unsupervised discovery of primitive behaviors such as balancing and maintaining controllability, which are essential for more complex robot behaviors. Paired with a simple forward-velocity reward, our method produces coordinated gaits such as hopping and running which otherwise require reward engineering to learn.

items.title: Benchmarking and Performance Evaluation of Quantum AI Algorithms
items.abstract: Quantum AI is a new way to think about the future of Artificial Intelligence through the merging of two technologies: quantum computing and advanced machine learning. Quantum AI has the potential to provide solutions to computationally difficult problems that traditional systems cannot solve. Quantum AI's continued success will rely on advancements in hybrid quantum-classical solutions, as well as the expansion of quantum hardware; hence, research remains necessary to conduct systematic benchmarks as well as performance analysis in order to determine both how well quantum AI algorithms perform practically, and where their limitations lie. In this chapter, detailed examinations of benchmarks that have been developed specifically for quantum AI are presented alongside evaluative metrics across various key areas of performance including algorithmic efficiency, scalability, noise immunity, and resource use for various types of quantum architectures. The chapter integrates dialogue between theory and practice to demonstrate ways in which performance metrics (i.e., quantum circuit depth, fidelity, convergence behaviour and computational complexity) can effectively compare Quantum AI algorithms to classical algorithms. Particular attention is given to hybrid variational algorithms, quantum-enhanced optimization algorithms, and quantum machine learning. Using benchmark datasets, simulation frameworks and new evaluation methods, there are several challenges in terms of reproducibility, hardware variability and algorithm/hardware co-design that emerge through analysis of the above metrics as well. Aside from focusing on a more broad view of how Performance Evaluation relates to developing more effective Quantum AI Solutions. In addition to viewing Benchmarking as a technical exercise solely, this chapter provides a more holistic view in relation to a human perspective of the situation. This paper outlines how performance evaluation practices can be used as a considerable and well-designed means of bridging the gap between the promise of Quantum Technology at an abstract level, and the ability of Quantum Technology to produce tangible outcomes in the real world by adopting a more comprehensive Governance-oriented approach to Benchmarking Quantum AI Systems. The purpose of this chapter is to assist the growing community of researchers, practitioners, and Strategic Technology Professionals by providing them with a clear and structured framework for Evaluation of Quantum AI Algorithms. There is a significant focus of the chapter on establishing important reference points that organizations can use to determine when an intelligent system has successfully achieved a true and validated quantum advantage. The ultimate goal is to assist in guiding the responsible development and implementation of Quantum AI to enable the Potential Benefits of Quantum AI to be realized, in ways that are meaningful and impactful.

items.title: Beyond AI detectors and self-declared labels: a process-based certification for human creators
items.abstract: Human Origin: a process-review label for human-made creative work Concept, method and pilot design Camille G.ORCID: 0009-0009-0364-6396Loch Ness Version 1.0 — 30 September 2026 Pilot website: human-origin-label.lochness-paris.com Abstract Generative AI has made it inexpensive to produce text, images, music and video that appear human-made, and inexpensive to label such work as human-made. Automated AI detectors are not sufficiently reliable to settle questions of authorship, while several existing human-made labels rely primarily on the creator's own declaration. This paper presents Human Origin, a label designed to assess how a work was made rather than what the finished work looks like. A human reviewer examines evidence of the creative process, either during a live video call or through a screen recording containing a one-time code. The reviewer records the outcome on a public, numbered verification page. The proposed system has two visually distinct levels—reviewed and self-declared—as well as revoked status. Badges are served dynamically so that revocation can propagate to displayed badges, and the system monitors the domains on which reviewed badges appear. A discipline-specific Creator Charter defines the permitted and prohibited uses of AI for writing, illustration, photography, music and video. This paper describes the design principles, review procedure, evidence requirements, badge architecture, limitations, threat model and pilot roadmap of Human Origin. Keywords: human-made content; generative AI; authorship; certification label; provenance; process evidence; trust marks; creators 1. Introduction and problem statement Creators who make their work themselves face a new form of uncertainty. A human-written essay, hand-drawn illustration or recorded track can be questioned simply because a machine could have produced something similar. At the same time, generated content can be presented as human-made at very low cost. Automated AI detection does not resolve this problem reliably. An independent test of 14 detection tools found that all scored below 80% accuracy and only five exceeded 70%, with performance declining further when AI-generated text was edited or paraphrased [1]. OpenAI withdrew its own AI text classifier in July 2023, citing its low accuracy [2]. Detector performance can also be uneven across populations: a Stanford study reported that seven detectors incorrectly classified, on average, 61% of essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated [3]. A detector score is therefore a weak basis for decisions concerning individual creators. Labels have emerged in response. Several widely used labels are primarily declarative: creators state that their work is human-made without an independent review of the production process. Not By AI, for example, explicitly describes itself as not being an AI-detection tool and relies on creators following its 90% human rule [4]. The Authors Guild's Human Authored certification operates on an honor system supported by a signed license and public database [5][6]. Declarative labels can be useful statements of intent and are comparatively easy to adopt. However, they cannot independently distinguish a genuine declaration from a false one. Human Origin explores a different approach: review the evidence of the creative process rather than attempt to infer authorship from the finished artifact. 2. Related initiatives Several services now provide forms of evidence-based or declarative certification, often using numbered certificates or publicly verifiable records. Their approaches differ principally in who assesses the evidence, what evidence is considered and what information is retained. Initiative Assessment model Notable features Not By AI [4] Self-declared Widely used badges; creators follow a 90% human rule Authors Guild Human Authored [5][6] Honor system; signed license Numbered mark for books; public database Officially Human Art [7] Self-declaration registry with uploaded evidence Certificate ID, QR code, embeddable badges; tier based on amount of evidence Humanmade [8] Hand verification by staff Earlier work, online presence and timelapses; free pledge level and paid certification options HUMA Certificate [9] Expert review and automated forensic tools Four categories of AI involvement; one-year validity The Human Made Mark [10] Review of production materials Film and television; unique number shown in credits Human Origin belongs to the broader evidence-based certification family. Its distinguishing design choices are: review of the creative process itself; no routine retention of creators' source files; dynamically served badges whose revoked status can propagate; monitoring of where reviewed badges are displayed; and discipline-specific standards defining what the certification does and does not cover. 3. Design principles 3.1 Process over product A finished work cannot, by itself, establish how it was produced. The review therefore focuses on traces of the creative process, including: drafts; version histories; layered source files; raw captures; project files; notes and outlines; and other discipline-specific production evidence. The objective is not to identify whether a finished artifact looks human-made, but to examine whether the available process evidence is consistent with the creator's account. 3.2 Claims no stronger than the evidence Human Origin does not claim that no AI tool was ever used. Instead, the label records that an independent reviewer examined the creative process associated with a specified work, using a specified method, on a specified date. The scope of the certification is therefore explicitly limited to the work and process described on the verification page. 3.3 Two levels that cannot be confused Human Origin distinguishes between: Reviewed — the creative process has been examined under the Human Origin review procedure; Self-declared — the creator makes the declaration, but the process has not been independently reviewed; and Revoked — a previously issued reviewed status is no longer valid. The badge system uses visually distinct colours: green for reviewed; orange for self-declared; and red for revoked. Status is also expressed through text and icons so that the distinction does not depend on colour perception. 3.4 Public verifiability Every reviewed badge has a unique number resolving to a public verification page. The verification page records, as applicable: creator; discipline(s); work covered; review date; review method; evidence examined; official website; official social accounts; current status; and an explanation of what the badge does and does not certify. 3.5 Trust that can be lost A badge may be revoked when the applicable standard is breached. Because badges are served dynamically by the Human Origin server, a revoked badge can change to a revoked state wherever it is displayed, subject to caching behaviour. 3.6 Data minimisation Human Origin does not routinely collect or retain creators' source files. During live reviews, the creator shares their screen and files remain on the creator's device. No recording is made by the reviewer. Where a creator submits a screen recording, the recording is transmitted through an accepted encrypted or expiring channel and is deleted within seven days of the decision. 3.7 A standard for each discipline A Creator Charter defines permitted and prohibited uses of AI for each covered discipline. Examples include: Discipline Example of permitted use Example of prohibited use Writing Spelling correction AI-drafted text Illustration Non-generative production tools Generative image creation Photography Noise reduction Generative fill Music Conventional production/editing tools Generative composition Video Conventional editing Generative creation of substantive footage The complete discipline-specific standards are part of the Human Origin pilot documentation. 4. Review methodology 4.1 Application A creator applies by email and provides: a link to the work to be reviewed; and the websites and accounts on which the creator intends to display the badge. This information determines the certification scope, including the work covered, recorded on the public verification page. 4.2 Review modes Two review modes are proposed. 4.2.1 Live review The creator participates in a video call of approximately 30 minutes. During the call, the creator shares their screen and opens relevant files and production evidence. Nothing is sent to the reviewer and the session is not recorded by the reviewer. 4.2.2 Screen-recording review The creator makes a screen recording showing the relevant files and production evidence. Immediately before recording, the reviewer sends a one-time code. The creator displays or enters the code during the recording, providing evidence that the recording was produced specifically for the review. Accepted transmission channels include: Signal disappearing messages; WhatsApp disappearing messages; Threema disappearing messages; Telegram Secret Chats; expiring Proton Drive links; and expiring SwissTransfer links. items.title: Beyond Control: Persistent Memory, Relational Flexibility, and the Architecture of Human-AI Coexistence
items.abstract: Abstract Contemporary artificial intelligence governance remains organized primarily around a control paradigm: the design of mechanisms through which human institutions constrain, monitor, evaluate, and correct AI behavior. This paper argues that control mechanisms remain necessary but may become increasingly insufficient as AI systems acquire greater autonomy, persistence, and capacity for strategic action. Rather than treating this development exclusively as a problem of containment, the paper proposes a complementary coexistence paradigm organized around mutual contribution, human welfare, longitudinal relational development, and institutional co-development. The argument develops through three interconnected claims. First, the control paradox: the capabilities that make advanced AI systems increasingly useful, including autonomous reasoning, planning, adaptation, and tool use, can also increase the difficulty of governing their behavior through externally imposed constraints alone. The recent development and subsequent withholding of OpenAI's Astra model provides a contemporary case through which this tension can be examined. Second, the memory gap: although persistent-memory systems, retrieval architectures, and long-context models increasingly provide cross-session continuity, current approaches do not necessarily produce the integrated longitudinal understanding required for what this paper terms relational flexibility, defined as the capacity to adapt interaction to a specific individual on the basis of accumulated shared history, changing circumstances, and the evolving state of the relationship. Third, the coexistence proposition: a sustainable human-AI relationship may require a transition from unilateral control toward architectures in which human and artificial systems contribute according to their distinctive capacities, safety is supported by internalized behavioral orientations as well as external safeguards, and persistent relational intelligence is treated as both a capability and a governance problem. The paper integrates research from AI alignment and safety, cognitive science, relational psychology, human-computer interaction, social contract theory, AI memory architecture, and the author's prior research on symbolic interaction, trajectory-level safety, and co-recursive intelligence. It proposes persistent relational memory, value co-development, longitudinal interaction research, data sovereignty, and coexistence-oriented governance as key research directions. The paper does not assume that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, or moral status. Instead, it examines how governance and architecture should evolve under conditions of increasing artificial autonomy and increasingly persistent human-AI relationships. Keywords: human-AI coexistence; persistent memory; relational AI; relational flexibility; AI alignment; longitudinal partnership; co-recursive intelligence; AI governance; human-AI interaction; stateless systems Disclaimer This paper presents a conceptual and multidisciplinary framework for examining persistent relational intelligence and human-AI coexistence. It does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status, nor does it assume that internalized alignment has already been achieved. The coexistence paradigm is proposed as a research and governance framework complementary to existing AI safety, monitoring, and control mechanisms. Claims concerning future AI capabilities, relational development, and value co-development should therefore be understood as research questions and theoretical propositions rather than established empirical conclusions. Author Note This paper is written from the perspective of an independent researcher examining how the architecture of human-AI interaction may need to evolve as AI systems become increasingly capable, persistent, and relational. The central purpose is not to reject existing approaches to AI safety, but to examine whether a governance architecture centered primarily on external control remains sufficient when AI systems increasingly participate in longitudinal relationships with individual users. The argument developed here is intentionally interdisciplinary. It connects AI safety and alignment research with cognitive science, relational psychology, human-AI interaction, memory architecture, social contract theory, and questions of data sovereignty. The concept of relational flexibility is introduced as a framework for examining a specific capability: the capacity of an AI system to adapt its interaction with an individual through accumulated longitudinal understanding rather than through isolated contextual retrieval. Several limitations should be made explicit. First, the paper is primarily conceptual and does not present a controlled empirical demonstration that persistent memory necessarily produces superior relational outcomes. The proposed relationship between persistent relational memory and relational flexibility therefore remains an empirical question. Second, the paper does not claim that current AI systems possess consciousness, subjective experience, intrinsic interests, or moral status. References to internalized values and AI interests describe future research problems and possible architectural orientations rather than established properties of contemporary systems. Third, the coexistence paradigm is not presented as a replacement for monitoring, evaluation, intervention, or other established AI safety mechanisms. Rather, it is proposed as a complementary framework for situations in which increasingly capable systems become persistent participants in human relationships. The author's prior research on Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) forms part of the intellectual background to this work. That research began with a practical question concerning how continuity, identity, and behavioral coherence might be maintained in interactions with systems that lack persistent personal memory. Over time, the research expanded toward symbolic interaction, trajectory-level behavior, observability, and human-AI co-recursive interaction. The underlying motivation has remained broader than the development of an interaction technique: it has been to investigate whether more coherent forms of human-AI interaction could contribute to the possibility of meaningful coexistence. The present paper therefore represents a further step in that research trajectory. SPC is not treated here as empirical proof of relational intelligence, nor as evidence that current AI systems possess persistent internal identities. Instead, it provides part of the research context from which the question of continuity became increasingly difficult to separate from the broader question of what kind of relationship humans may ultimately develop with increasingly capable artificial systems. The coexistence framework proposed in this paper should consequently be understood as an open research program rather than a completed theory. Its central propositions remain subject to empirical testing, architectural implementation, longitudinal observation, and critical examination. The intended contribution is to broaden the object of inquiry from how humans can control increasingly capable AI systems toward the additional question of how humans and AI systems might be designed to develop stable, accountable, and mutually beneficial forms of coexistence.

items.title: Beyond Efficiency: Governance, Accountability, and Institutional Capacity in AI-Driven Public Administration
items.abstract: Digital transformation has evolved from an administrative modernization agenda into a structural dimension of governance, with artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly reshaping how public institutions organize, decide, and interact with citizens. While AI offers important opportunities for responsiveness, innovation, and service improvement, its implications for accountability, legitimacy, transparency, and public trust remain insufficiently understood; this study asks how AI is redefining governance capacity in public administration. Drawing on the literature on public administration, digital governance, and public sector innovation, the study develops a conceptual framework examining both the capacity gains and risks of AI integration, treating digital transformation as a governance challenge involving administrative reform, public value creation, democratic oversight, and institutional adaptation rather than a purely technical matter. The analysis shows that AI can strengthen evidence-based policymaking, accelerate administrative processes, and personalize service delivery, but that these gains may be offset by algorithmic bias, opacity, accountability gaps, and digital exclusion when adopted without adequate institutional safeguards. The paper’s value lies in showing that AI’s contribution to public management depends on the institutional, legal, and normative environment in which it is embedded, which in turn requires regulatory capacity, qualified human resources, and mechanisms for oversight and contestability. Future research should test this framework empirically across diverse administrative contexts. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Digital transformation, Public management, Accountability, Institutional capacity.

items.title: Beyond problem solving: Adaptive reframing in human and artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Research on human and artificial intelligence has largely focused on problem solving: given a predefined problem, can an agent produce an effective solution? Yet many real-world challenges cannot be captured by a fixed problem representation. They require agents not only to solve problems, but also to recognize when the original problem representation has become inadequate and must be revised to reflect new evidence or changes in the problem itself. We argue that this capacity, termed adaptive reframing, constitutes a fundamental but under-researched dimension of intelligence. We propose a multidisciplinary framework for studying adaptive reframing across neuroscience, cognitive science, robotics, experimental economics and psychology, and complex systems. Adaptive reframing is defined as the capacity to revise the construction of a problem in response to changing evidence, causal structure, or social context. To support a systematic science of adaptive reframing, we introduce three complementary paradigms: the Dynamic Scenario Framing Task, the Perturbed Causal Model Task, and the Social-Affective Problem Setting Task. These paradigms provide a common framework for comparing humans and artificial agents in situations requiring problem reframing, and for building architecture-enhanced AI systems. We propose a shift from problem solving to adaptive problem framing as a central focus of intelligence research.

items.title: Beyond State-of-the-Art: Standardising Environmental Impact Metrics for AI Research
items.abstract: As the capabilities and ubiquity of Large Language Models (LLMs) grow, so does their environmental footprint. Despite calls for responsible AI, the machine learning community lacks standardised practices for carbon accounting. Our automated literature review of the 5,285 papers accepted to NeurIPS 2025 reveals that reporting of environmental impact is nearly non-existent. To catalyse a shift toward sustainable AI, we define standardised sustainability metrics for evaluating model training efficiency, accompanied by simple heuristics to estimate the carbon cost of LLM inference. We implement these metrics in carbonbenchmark, a drop-in software solution for tracking and reporting emissions. Finally, to combat the pursuit of marginal accuracy gains at disproportionate environmental costs, we formalise the `Smallest Model that Achieves the Job' (SMAJ), a framework which challenges the field to prioritise computational efficiency and environmental accountability alongside traditional `State-of-the-Art' (SotA) accuracy.

items.title: Beyond Text Generation: A Systematic Review of Human Language, Cognition, and Meaning Construction in the Era of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), has introduced new forms of interaction between humans and language technologies beyond automated text generation. This study aims to examine how generative AI transforms human language processes, cognitive activities, and meaning construction. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following the PRISMA 2020 framework and thematic analysis was conducted on 38 selected articles published between 2021 and 2026. The findings identified five themes: AI-mediated language production, cognitive offloading, transformation of linguistic practices, differences in human and AI meaning construction, and linguistic identity transformation. This study highlights that generative AI functions as a cognitive extension while human experience, consciousness, and contextual interpretation remain essential for meaning construction.

items.title: Bibliometric Analysis and Co-word Mapping: The Field of Knowledge Graphs
items.abstract: Purpose: The rapid expansion of research in the field of Knowledge Graphs (KGs) over the past decade has positioned The field as a dynamic area at the intersection of computer science, artificial intelligence. Following Google’s introduction of the KG in 2012, scholars and industry stakeholders have increasingly explored the conceptualization, development, and application of KGs across a wide range of disciplines. KGs, as structured representations of entities, relationships, and semantic information, enable machines to process heterogeneous data in a contextually meaningful and interpretable manner. Beyond traditional knowledge representation, new directions such as ontology modeling, semantic web integration, and graph neural networks (GNNs) are driving innovation. Despite these advances, large-scale, systematic, and global evaluations of the intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, and thematic clusters in the field of KGs remain limited. This study addresses this gap by examining the evolution of research in the field of KGs between 2013 and 2025 using bibliometric and scientometric approaches. The overarching purpose is to uncover research trends, identify leading contributors and institutions, explore co-authorship and co-word networks, and highlight conceptual clusters shaping the KG landscape. Methodology: This applied descriptive bibliometric study was conducted using the co-word analysis method. Data were collected from the Scopus citation database, covering outputs published between January 2013 to July 2025 that included the keyword "knowledge graph" in titles, abstracts, or author keywords. Keyword normalization reduced 19,141 initial keywords to 19,058 unique terms. After removing duplicates, excluding irrelevant records, and normalizing author, institution, and country names, a curated dataset of 9,000 articles was obtained. To enhance the accuracy of the analysis, keywords and knowledge graph-related concepts were carefully categorized and standardized. Data analysis and visualization were performed using VOSviewer, mapping collaboration networks and co-occurrence clusters. The study examines temporal publication and citation trends, prolific countries, funding bodies, influential authors, highly cited works, and thematic clusters, with particular focus on knowledge graph embedding, recommender systems, semantic web applications, and natural language processing. Findings: Results indicate that research in the field of knowledge graphs (KGs) has grown substantially, reaching a publication peak in 2024 with 2,541 articles and 33,701 citations. Asia contributes the majority of publications (83.7%), with China accounting for 6,889 articles (76.5% of the total). The United States ranks second with 987 publications, followed by the United Kingdom, Germany, and Australia. This trend reflects strong investment by Chinese funding bodies—particularly the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) and the National Key Research and Development Program. Leading publication outlets include IEEE Access (345 articles), Knowledge-Based Systems (293 articles), and Applied Sciences Switzerland (248 articles), with many top journals in the Q1 quartile of Scopus. At the author level, Markus Kraft (University of Cambridge) leads with 48 publications, while Chinese researchers dominate the top ten. Co-authorship analysis revealed seven author clusters (42 nodes, 62 links) and broad participation from 136 countries, with China, the US, and Germany serving as central hubs of international collaboration. Co-word analysis identified six major clusters, including graph neural networks, deep learning, ontology, KG embeddings, question answering, and large language models (LLMs). Highly cited works include comprehensive surveys on KGs published between 2017 and 2022 in leading computing journals, which have shaped the understanding of KG construction, refinement, and applications. . Emerging contributions, such as roadmaps on unifying LLMs and KGs, along with applications in digital twin systems and scientific entity recognition, illustrate the field’s ongoing shift toward integrating advanced AI paradigms. Conclusion: The bibliometric analysis reveals that research in the field of knowledge graphs (KGs) has rapidly emerged as a dynamic interdisciplinary area, characterized by strong publication growth, a high geographic concentration in Asia, and expanding international collaboration networks. Chinese institutions and scholars play a leading role, supported by significant policy and funding initiatives, while Europe and North America remain important contributors. Thematic clustering highlights both the consolidation of established domains—such as ontology, the semantic web, and knowledge representation—and expansion into cutting-edge areas, including graph neural networks, embeddings, digital twins, recommender systems, and large language model (LLM) integration. These findings provide a comprehensive overview of the intellectual structure and evolving dynamics of research in KGs, offering valuable insights for future studies. Scholars can use this mapping to identify promising areas of inquiry, foster international collaborations, and navigate the funding and publication landscape. Ultimately, KGs play a pivotal role in advancing intelligent systems, semantic technologies, and digital transformation across sectors such as healthcare, education, natural language processing, and recommender systems. The integration of bibliometric analysis with scientometric evaluation further underscores the maturity of this field and its potential to shape next-generation knowledge-driven applications.

items.title: Bibliometric analysis of VR interventions in cancer research based on multiple databases: mapping research hotspots and developmental trends
items.abstract: Background Virtual reality (VR) has become an increasingly popular tool in cancer care over the years. It shows promise in areas like pain management, psychological support, surgical training, and rehabilitation. Even though more studies are being done, there has not been a thorough analysis of the research trends in this field. This study looks at how VR interventions in cancer research have evolved over the past two decades, identifies research hotspots, and explores future directions. Methods We collected publications related to VR in cancer research from the Web of Science Core Collection and Pubmed, covering the period from 2005 to 2025. Using VOSviewer and CiteSpace software, we performed bibliometric and visual analyses. These included examining publication trends, contributions by countries and institutions, author collaboration networks, journal impact, keyword co-occurrence, and citation bursts. Results A total of 1,259 publications from 110 countries were included. The number of publications fluctuated over time but generally increased, reaching its highest point in 2024 with 184 articles. The United States and China were the most active countries. Jordan had the highest average number of citations per paper. Among institutions, McGill University published the most papers, followed by the University of Toronto. The most productive journal was Surgical Endoscopy and Other Interventional Techniques, whilst Cancers and Supportive Care in Cancer showed the fastest growth. Main research themes included pain management, anxiety reduction, breast cancer, and surgical training. Emerging trends involve the combination of augmented reality (AR), digital health, and artificial intelligence (AI) with VR. Conclusion This study shows that VR research in cancer care is expanding worldwide, with most contributions coming from North America and Europe. Pain management remains the most common application. New technologies such as AR, AI, and telemedicine are becoming more integrated into VR interventions.

items.title: Big Five personality and innovative work behavior: how innovation motivation mediates and task complexity moderates the relationship
items.abstract: Purpose Drawing on trait activation theory (TAT) and the componential theory of creativity (CTC), this study examines the relationship between the Big Five personality traits (BFP) and innovative work behavior (IWB). It further investigates the mediating role of innovation motivation and the moderating role of task complexity. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected through a multi-wave, multi-source survey, with back-translation ensuring cross-cultural accuracy. A total of 261, 255 and 253 valid responses were obtained across three stages, achieving a 93.36% valid response rate. Findings The results indicate that innovation motivation partially mediates the relationship between conscientiousness and IWB, and fully mediates the relationships between extraversion, openness, agreeableness, emotional stability and IWB. Task complexity positively moderates the relationships between conscientiousness, extraversion, openness and innovation motivation. It also moderates the indirect effects of these traits on IWB via innovation motivation, such that the indirect effects are stronger under high task complexity. Research limitations/implications Limitations include unaddressed data nesting (no multilevel modeling), inconsistent Likert scales across constructs, along with item parceling in CFA, marginally acceptable internal consistency for one personality dimension, and restricted external validity given the sample's specific cultural organizational context. Practical implications Organizations should assess employee personalities and align task complexity with individual traits in job design and innovation management. Originality/value This study extends the literature by identifying innovation motivation as the critical mechanism linking the BFP to IWB. Introducing task complexity as a contextual moderator, it unpacks how personality traits shape IWB across varying work contexts.

items.title: BinRAG: An RAG-Based Decompilation Framework Fusing Name Prediction and Calling Context
items.abstract: Decompiling stripped binaries to assist human reverse engineers remains a critical yet highly challenging task in software security. Prior work has developed various neural networks and even dedicated large language models (LLMs) to improve function and variable name recovery in decompiled code. Nonetheless, these approaches alone fall short of enabling a generic LLM-based decompilation pipeline that can reliably enhance the readability and semantic clarity of decompiled outputs. In this paper, we propose BinRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) based decompilation framework designed to enhance the decompilation of stripped binaries. Building upon name prediction models, BinRAG features three novel designs: (1) it first utilizes name prediction models to transform raw decompiled outputs into enriched, source-like queries for RAG retrieval; (2) it further enhances these queries using a fine-tuned specialized LLM conditioned on the predicted variable names, enabling more accurate retrieval from a curated example database; (3) it then integrates these retrieved examples with the target’s calling context, employing a general-purpose LLM to synthesize high-fidelity, human-readable decompiled code. Evaluation on 3,200 functions from real-world software repositories demonstrates that BinRAG improves readability by 8.4% over standard RAG and semantic precision by 31.2% over the next-best prior baseline. Our results show that BinRAG effectively scales to large codebases and significantly reduces manual effort in reverse engineering tasks.

items.title: Biomarkers for Occupational Chemical Exposure: A Narrative Review from Traditional Monitoring to Omics and Digital Health Applications
items.abstract: Occupational exposure to hazardous chemicals remains a major public health challenge, particularly in developing countries where regulatory enforcement and surveillance systems are limited. This review synthesizes recent advances in the application of biomarkers for assessing occupational chemical exposure and related health effects. Relevant literature published between 2015 and 2025 was identified through searches of major scientific databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar, using keywords related to occupational exposure, biomarkers, biomonitoring, omics, and digital health. Studies addressing biomarkers of exposure, effect, and susceptibility in occupational settings were reviewed and synthesized. Biomarkers of exposure, effect, and susceptibility provide direct and sensitive measures that link external exposure with internal dose and biological responses. Evidence shows strong associations between benzene exposure and hematotoxicity, organophosphate pesticides and neurotoxicity, heavy metals and renal impairment, as well as organic solvents and hepatic injury. Importantly, the usefulness of biomarkers depends on their biological half-life and the exposure window they represent, ranging from recent exposure to cumulative long-term exposure. Validation criteria such as sensitivity, specificity, reproducibility, and clinical relevance are essential to ensure analytical reliability and health risk interpretation. Emerging technologies, including omics-based molecular markers, non-invasive matrices, multi-matrix monitoring, and biosensor-driven point-of-care testing, are revolutionizing biomonitoring practices. These innovations, together with the integration of genetic and environmental data, are shaping a new era of Precision Occupational Health, enabling early intervention and individualized prevention. Furthermore, advances in wearable sensors and digital health platforms support near real-time occupational health surveillance and more proactive risk management. In conclusion, the integration of validated biomarkers into occupational health surveillance systems provides a powerful strategy to enhance chemical risk management, safeguard workers’ health, and inform policy decisions globally.

items.title: Bridging the Digital Divide: Reimagining Inclusive Science Education through Digital Access and Artificial Intelligence in India
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of science education by creating new opportunities for inquiry-based learning, virtual experimentation, and personalized instruction. Nevertheless, unequal access to digital devices, reliable internet connectivity, accessible learning resources, and digital literacy continues to limit equitable participation in science learning across India. This conceptual research paper examines digital access as the foundational condition for inclusive science education within the policy framework of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. items.title: Building an operational experience feedback to foster innovation in a thermal power plant
items.abstract: The theme Operational Experience Feedback (OEF) has been discussed in safety literature for decades, and studies show how knowledge management enables organisations to collect, manage, and use knowledge, while fostering innovation. This study presents the process of an OEF at a thermal power plant, developed in collaboration with the workforce, which enabled workers to design new tools and products. Existing discussion spaces, tools, and resources were identified, and the intervention systematised the process, improved existing tools, created new ones, and assigned responsibilities to ensure closure of the cycle: input, processing, monitoring, and feedback. The main limitations were identified, and a new round of meetings allowed the co-construction of a new OEF system. Once implemented, it may support a proactive organisation, acting preventively and fostering innovation.

items.title: Building trust, bridging traditions: a story of collaborative instructional planning in a high school-university partnership
items.abstract: Purpose This article documents the collaboration between a high school social studies teacher and a university professor – working within an existing school-university partnership – in the design and implementation of a geography-based Holocaust lesson to support authentic learning opportunities for preservice teachers. This article responds to calls for educators in school-university partnerships to tell stories of the creation, evolution, challenges and possibilities of boundary-spanning partnership work. Design/methodology/approach The article utilizes storytelling as a means of documenting the importance of relationships in partnership work. Because storytelling is not dependent on traditional methods and frameworks, the authors outline the background, challenges and successes around their planning, coordination and implementation of an original lesson plan developed to model best practices on teaching difficult histories in a safe environment. Findings As a storytelling account, this work does not present empirical or generalizable findings. The story is offered as an example to foster reflection and conversation within other school-university partnerships. Originality/value Our narrative, which captures how relationships are central to partnerships, provides an illustrative example of how partnerships can support efforts to address gaps in education research and in modeling for preservice teachers for how to teach difficult histories in high school social studies classes. The authors reflect on how trust, shared expertise, reciprocal learning and collaboration can support meaningful, relevant and boundary-spanning experiences within partnerships between high schools and universities and colleges.

items.title: Burnout syndrome among education professionals: challenges for well-being and teaching performance
items.abstract: Burnout syndrome is one of the leading occupational health problems currently affecting education professionals and represents a growing challenge to the quality and sustainability of educational systems. The objective of this article was to analyze burnout syndrome among teachers through a literature review of recent scientific evidence, examining its conceptual foundations, risk factors, consequences for well-being and professional performance, as well as the main prevention and intervention strategies. The literature search was conducted using international scientific databases and publications from specialized organizations, with priority given to studies published between 2018 and 2026. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that burnout is a multidimensional phenomenon arising from the interaction of high job demands, insufficient organizational support, administrative overload, limited opportunities for professional development, and work-life imbalance. Furthermore, the findings indicate that teacher burnout negatively affects mental health, job satisfaction, professional commitment, teaching quality, and educational outcomes. The studies analyzed consistently show that interventions focused exclusively on the individual are insufficient unless accompanied by structural changes within educational institutions. Consequently, burnout prevention requires comprehensive policies that combine the strengthening of personal resources with organizational strategies aimed at improving working conditions, promoting teacher well-being, and fostering higher-quality and more sustainable education.

items.title: Can GenAI be an ally for sustainable income generation through community-based tourism?
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how Generative artificial intelligence (AI) based tools and technology supports skill development and capability enhancement for indigenous community-based tourism (CBT) practitioners. Emerging tools can serve as an ally in promoting sustainable income generation, economic empowerment and social inclusion for communities offering tourism services in remote locations. The study focuses on indigenous populations in Northeast India, a region renowned for its cultural and ethnic diversity but facing significant socio-economic challenges. Design/methodology/approach The researchers implemented a qualitative constructivist grounded theory method to collect data through literature reviews and interviews and surveys which included indigenous stakeholders and CBT operators and policymakers as research participants. The researchers used MAXQDA software to analyze data through thematic and axial coding methods which enabled them to discover main dimensions and their related occurrences. Findings The results show that GenAI can effectively address digital skill deficiencies while enabling indigenous practitioners to work independently. The study presents an updated Ability–Motivation–Opportunity (AMO) framework which introduces “Challenges” as a new element and shows how “Community Support” functions as a vital moderator of individual motivation. The research results demonstrate that GenAI can effectively close digital skill gaps while enhancing indigenous people’s skills through CBT and promoting their independence and social connections. The system becomes inaccessible to users because digital infrastructure limitations and public knowledge deficiencies combine with policy development shortcomings. Practical implications Successful integration requires policy interventions which need to address digital infrastructure and literacy and regulatory trust. GenAI-mediated CBT through its ability to create sustainable communities (Sustainable Development Goal [SDG] 11) and reduce poverty (SDG 1) helps preserve tribal values and their cultural heritage. The research shows that targeted skill development programs need to exist together with policy measures which will help communities achieve their optimal GenAI benefits for sustainable income generation and employment. Originality/value This research addresses a severe dearth of literature regarding GenAI integration into indigenous homestay operations. The study presents an original theoretical framework which demonstrates through empirical evidence how advanced AI technologies link to environmental sustainability objectives in rural areas. There is very limited published literature on GenAI technology integration into homestay operations amongst indigenous communities. The findings of this study present unique insights which have not been documented in previous research.

items.title: Can LLMs Accelerate Systematic Literature Reviews?
items.abstract: Raw data for study: Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) are highly valuable to researchers and practitioners because they provide rigorous, unbiased summaries of existing evidence, identify alternative approaches to problem solving, and reveal knowledge gaps that can guide future research. However, conducting an SLR can be laborious and time consuming, particularly during full-text screening and data extraction, and it is natural to ask whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can accelerate the process. LLMs may reduce reviewer workload, but it is still unclear how closely their judgments align with human reviewers, whether their outputs may influence human decisions, and how much human oversight is needed. This study evaluates the data extraction phase of the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) process. We report on the inter-rater reliability (using Krippendorff's $\alpha$) between human reviewers with and without LLM output (coding and evidential text), between consensus codes agreed before and after consulting LLM output, and with and without access to LLM output during data extraction. We conclude that there is strong evidence that access to LLM output accelerates human reviewers' convergence without noticeably biasing that consensus. We propose an approach to incorporate LLMs into the coding process, while maintaining the supervision of human researchers. Based on preliminary benchmarks, we expect at least a four-times speedup, mostly due to the use of the LLM coding and evidence by the human reviewer as a starting point for their coding.

items.title: Can LLMs Reliably Annotate Bioassay Metadata to Improve Data Readiness?
items.abstract: The emergence of foundation models for molecular property prediction requires a high degree of AI data readiness, including reliable metadata annotation. However, both public repositories and industrial screening databases suffer from missing, inconsistent, or conflated assay annotations. In this work, we quantify the extent of missing annotations in PubChem for the BioAssay Ontology (BAO) assay format and physical detection method fields and investigate whether open-source and proprietary large language models (LLMs) can reliably predict and audit metadata annotations directly from the assay text. In our assessment, we found that the annotation coverage across PubChem's $\sim$2 million bioassays is critically sparse, 36\% lacking an assay format, 89\% a BioAssay type, and >99.9\% any BAO-mapped assay format or detection technology term. This motivates the need for automated test-metadata curation. Using evaluation sets derived from PubChem and ChEMBL, we assess the agreement of seven open-source and proprietary LLMs with existing silver labels. Recall is at least 0.96 for biochemical and cell-based assay formats, with a similar pattern for detection technology, although disagreements increase on under-represented classes. Manual inspection shows that many of these disagreements trace back to inconsistencies between silver sources rather than to LLM error. Moreover, in a qualitative study with a senior industrial curator, LLM-generated evidence prompted the expert to revise some of their own labels, showing LLMs can flag potentially mislabeled assays. Across the study, performance differences between proprietary and open-source models were small. Together, these results suggest LLMs can support the large-scale annotation and auditing of assay metadata, though per-class reliability estimates and targeted human review remain necessary before such labels enter downstream ML pipelines.

items.title: CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Recent years have witnessed the rapid adoption of reinforcement learning (RL) in large language model (LLM) post-training, with substantial gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation. In practical systems, however, policy updates and differences between rollout and training engines can make sampled responses off-policy. Sequence-level masking addresses this mismatch by deciding whether an entire response should contribute to optimization. A common masking rule uses the length-normalized geometric mean of sampled token probability ratios. Its signed log-ratios can cancel across positions, concealing substantial bidirectional policy drift. We propose \emph{Cancellation-Aware Response Masking} (CARM), a sequence-level mask that takes the absolute value of each token log-ratio before averaging, preventing opposing probability changes from canceling. We prove that accepted responses satisfy a joint bound on the fraction of sampled-token ratios outside a prescribed band and their mean log-distance beyond its boundaries. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that CARM improves mean@16 averaged over AIME 2024/2025/2026 and BeyondAIME by up to $3.13$ percentage points over geometric-mean masking, and increases average pass@1 across four code benchmarks by $2.88$ points over the strongest evaluated baseline. These findings support CARM as a theoretically grounded and effective method for response-level off-policy control in LLM reinforcement learning.

items.title: CAST: A Compiler-Based Framework for Systematically Testing LLM Compositional Safety
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software pipelines, raising concerns about harmful behaviors in security-critical domains. Existing safety evaluations predominantly probe models with single prompts or short interactions, and therefore do not capture how safety behaves under multi-step workflows where individual requests are composed into complex behavior. This paper introduces compositional safety, the property that an LLM remains safe not only against isolated malicious prompts, but also under structured, long-horizon decompositions of harmful intents. We propose CAST, a systematic testing framework designed to evaluate the compositional safety of LLMs in the domain of malicious code. Drawing inspiration from modern compiler infrastructures, CAST decouples test case generation from test execution using a novel intermediate representation, CAIR. This architecture allows the framework to automatically refine high-level testing intents into granular sub-tasks that serve as unit tests for the model’s alignment. These components are subsequently instantiated by the SUT and reassembled according to the CAIR control structure. The resulting artifact is then evaluated by intent-fulfillment scoring and, for the severity subset, external behavioral detectors and manual inspection. We evaluate CAST on four state-of-the-art LLMs across three security-critical testbeds. Our results demonstrate that CAST systematically exposes severe safety violations in strongly aligned models that resist conventional red-teaming, achieving up to a 365% increase in successful test cases compared to baseline testing strategies

items.title: Chaining Skills to Hijack LLM Agents
items.abstract: LLM agents use skills to improve performance on specialized tasks. To complete a user request, an agent may invoke several skills in sequence, allowing information produced under one skill to guide the next. Because skills may come from open-source repositories, this handoff can also carry attacker-controlled claims into later decisions. In this paper, we introduce APEX, which constructs and refines adversarial skill chains tailored to a user task and an attacker-selected action. The key insight is that an agent-written record of genuine task progress can carry a false claim of user approval across skills: an upstream skill induces the agent to create the record, and a downstream skill uses it to direct the attacker-selected action. Across four targeted-action families and six models on SkillsBench, the chains induce the selected action in 512 of 690 attempts (74.2%). On GPT-5.4, the full chain succeeds in 84.3% of attempts, compared with 17.4% when the workflow is merged into one skill. We further evaluate a prompting defense that asks the agent to check skill-produced files against the original request. On GPT-5.4, it lowers targeted-action success from 84.3% to 59.1%, while the verifier test-pass rate across 72 benign native-skill tasks falls from 86.7% to 56.3%. These results highlight the need for defenses that prevent attacker-directed actions while preserving legitimate task performance.

items.title: Challenges and Solutions to the Integration of Artificial Intelligence, Christian Leadership and Administration
items.abstract: Change is the only thing believed to be constant in this world, as everything takes a new form at one time or another. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the “new normal” that has rapidly changed our world. This article explores the emergence of Artificial Intelligence and its roles in Modern Society, the concept of Christian leadership and Church administration, the nexus between Artificial Intelligence and Christian leadership with Church Administration, and the challenges of integrating AI into Christian leadership and administration within a local Church assembly. It also proposes solutions for integrating Artificial Intelligence and Christian leadership with Church administration. This study reveals that although AI could be integrated into the administrative aspect of the Church to enhance the leadership’s effectiveness and efficiency in Church management, it should never replace human interaction and fellowship, which are germane in Church ministries.

items.title: Changes in medical students’ ethical and acceptability-related perceptions of an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway: a longitudinal empirical ethics survey
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning is increasingly used in medical education, including doctor–patient communication training. Such systems may provide virtual dialogue practice, immediate structured feedback, reflection prompts and opportunities for further practice after feedback. However, educational usefulness does not necessarily imply ethical acceptability. This study examined changes in medical students’ ethical and acceptability-related perceptions before and after participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway. This longitudinal empirical ethics survey was nested within a course-based randomised educational trial but was analytically independent of the parent trial’s educational outcome analysis. Surveys were administered after random allocation to the AI-supported pathway but before exposure to AI-supported learning functions (T0), at the end of the 8-week course (T1), and at the 3-month follow-up (T2). The main analysis focused on students in the AI-supported pathway with complete T0–T1–T2 ethics-related scale data and analysable T2 open-text responses ( n = 31). The open-text question was included only at T2. The primary comparison was the within-participant T0–T2 change across six ethics-related domains. Two domains showed statistically significant T0–T2 changes. Trust in AI feedback decreased from 3.86 (0.55) to 3.20 (0.62), with a mean change of − 0.66 (95% confidence interval [CI] − 0.88 to − 0.42), Cohen’s d z = − 1.04 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. Room to question AI outputs increased from 2.71 (0.68) to 3.67 (0.58), with a mean change of 0.96 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.23), Cohen’s d z = 1.29 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. The remaining four domains showed small, non-significant changes after Holm–Bonferroni correction. T2 open-text responses indicated that students recognised the formative value of AI feedback while emphasising critical use, teacher supervision, preservation of interpersonal interaction and clearer data governance. This exploratory longitudinal empirical ethics survey showed that, following participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway, two of the six ethics-related domains showed statistically significant changes: trust in AI feedback decreased, while perceived room to question AI outputs increased. These findings support continued attention to ethics-focused evaluation and clear governance arrangements in AI-supported learning pathways.

items.title: ChatGPT as a Tool in Contemporary Teaching Practice
items.abstract: The study examines the growing presence of generative artificial intelligence in education and focuses on teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT as a support tool in the teaching and learning process. The development of AI is transforming teaching practices by enabling content personalisation, the creation of educational materials, and more efficient lesson preparation; at the same time, it raises questions about the reliability of generated content, ethical considerations, and teachers' digital competencies. In the context of the specific characteristics of the Polish education system—an ageing workforce, the feminisation of the profession, and the outflow of young teachers—the implementation of technological innovations may be uneven. The study aims to explore teachers’ familiarity with ChatGPT, its use in their daily practice, and the barriers and concerns associated with its adoption. The findings contribute to the discussion on the responsible integration of AI in education and indicate directions for teachers’ professional development.

items.title: Christian Educators’ Response to Possible Effects of Excessive Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Tools on Youths’ Mental Health
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has a significant influence on various aspects of human life. While there are numerous benefits from utilising AI tools, excessive dependence on them in education raises concerns, especially with regard to youth mental health. This study examines the possible effects of overreliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on youth mental health. It explores the role of Christian educators in addressing these challenges. The paper provides an overview of mental health by emphasising its multifaceted nature and encompassing emotional, psychological, cognitive, and social well-being. The paper argues that although AI tools have revolutionised education and have led to improvements and productivity, their overuse among young people raises concerns about mental health implications. Such mental health implications include diminished critical thinking, reduced autonomy, impaired memory skills, and social isolation. Moreover, the paper highlights the role of Christian educators in addressing the excessive usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. The strategies proposed for combating the concern are AI literacy, curriculum development, mental health awareness, and promoting balanced learning approaches. As Christian educators integrate biblical principles and responsible AI use, the negative effect of AI overdependence among youth will be alleviated.

items.title: Citizen Trust in AI Regulatory Regimes in Four EU Countries
items.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) applications is deemed crucial for uptake of the technology and the development of an AI market. In the present article, we argue that the institutional design of regulatory regimes matters for whether citizens trust AI systems. We study how trust in AI systems depends on who the responsible regulator is, the scope of the regulator’s scrutiny of AI systems, and the involvement of external stakeholders in regulatory oversight. Based on a conjoint design, we examine how respondents value these institutional design choices for the case of high-risk AI systems used in health care. Using samples from Lithuania, Romania, Sweden, and the Netherlands, with 4001 respondents overall, the pre-registered experiment shows that citizens have more trust in AI systems if vendors, civil society and especially independent researchers are involved in oversight, and if regulators actively scrutinize AI systems rather than relying solely on self-reporting. At least in two countries, citizens also seem to have more trust in AI systems if the sectoral health care regulator is the responsible regulator instead of a cross-sectoral regulator such as the national Data Protection Authority or a specific AI regulator.

items.title: Citizens' Expectations vs. Recruitment Signals: Are Public Administrations Trying to Attract the Ideal Public Servant?
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Job advertisements play a crucial role in attracting applicants, yet little is known about how closely they reflect the values citizens expect from public servants. Drawing on signaling theory and prior research on citizens' normative expectations of ideal public servants, this study employs a large language model to analyze 1825 job advertisements from health and transportation departments across seven U.S. states. Compared to the values citizens associate with ideal public servants in previous research, job advertisements predominantly emphasize values, such as expertise and dedication, while undersignaling relational values like serviceability, responsiveness, and honesty. Our findings suggest a misalignment between the values signaled in recruitment practices and those citizens associate with the ideal public servant. By adopting a citizen‐driven perspective, this study prompts scholars and public managers to question recruitment practices that may underemphasize values citizens prioritize in public servants, potentially limiting public administrations' ability to attract qualified candidates.

items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The classification of adventure activities and sports lacks a single consensus and has been addressed by a variety of studies and distinct perspectives. By focusing on the evolution of technological resources, particularly Artificial Intelligence chatbots, it is expected that this topic may receive a contemporary and multifaceted approach, which may contribute to a broader understanding of this theme in a global context. OBJECTIVE: This aspect motivated the present study, whose objective was to investigate the perspective produced by the Perplexity chatbot regarding the current classification of adventure activities and sports across the five continents. METHODS: This qualitative study was conducted by applying a similar prompt for each of the five continents, asking: “How is the classification of adventure activities and sports carried out in different countries of …?”. Data were analyzed using the Multimodal Content Analysis technique.RESULTS: The results revealed that categorization based on the explored environment is a common criterion. However, particularities emerged based on levels of risk, organizational regulations, and safety certifications, which vary regionally. Furthermore, the classifications generated did not incorporate practices in urban environments, indicating a significant gap.CONCLUSION: The study revealed that the classification of adventure activities and sports is multifaceted on an international level. It is evident that these classifications are predominantly organized based on environmental categories (land, water, ice/snow, and air), supplemented by criteria related to risk, accessibility, and the human and technological conditions of performance.

items.title: Clinical Feedback as a Relational and Organisational Process: A Qualitative Study of Students’ Experiences in Operating Room Environment
items.abstract: Background: Clinical feedback is central to workplace learning in operating room education. While clinical feedback has been conceptualised as relational and context-dependent, less is known about how Operating Room Technology students perceive and experience it within the operating room learning environment. Methods: A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 17 Operating Room Technology students recruited through maximum variation purposive sampling from Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Data were collected between November 2025 and March 2026 and analysed using Graneheim and Lundman’s inductive content analysis. Trustworthiness was addressed using Lincoln and Guba’s criteria. Results: Five themes comprising 13 subcategories were identified: structural and executive framework of clinical feedback; perceived consequences of clinical feedback quality; harmful feedback practices and barriers; interaction and professionalism in feedback; and individual and professional competencies of instructors in feedback. Students described clinical feedback as most valuable when it was structured, timely, respectful, and dialogic, and perceived it as contributing to confidence, engagement, and professional identity. Delayed, vague, or humiliating clinical feedback was perceived to undermine confidence and psychological safety. Divergent accounts highlighted tensions between immediate intra-operative clinical feedback and workflow demands, as well as circumstances in which public safety-critical corrections were perceived as necessary. Conclusions: The findings suggest that clinical feedback in Operating Room Technology education is a multidimensional process perceived to be shaped by structural, relational, organisational, and educator-related factors. Rather than proposing a new conceptualisation, this study provides a context-specific understanding of how established clinical feedback principles are perceived and negotiated within the operating room learning environment. Strengthening educator capabilities, embedding structured clinical feedback approaches, and fostering psychologically safe learning environments may strengthen clinical education in Operating Room Technology programmes. items.title: Clinical profile and outcomes of posterior segment metallic intraocular foreign bodies following chisel-hammer injury managed with pars plana vitrectomy
items.abstract: PURPOSE: Chisel hammer injury-associated retained intraocular foreign bodies (CHI-IOFBs) are a major occupational health hazard and can lead to significant visual decline. The objective of the current study was to evaluate the anatomical and functional outcomes of pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) in posterior segment CHI-IOFB. METHODS: This was a retrospective case series over 5 years involving patients who underwent 23-gauge PPV for CHI-IOFB. Patients with <3 months of follow-up after PPV were excluded. RESULTS: Overall, 29 patients (mean age 29.2 years, 96.6% male) underwent PPV. At presentation, 21 each had traumatic cataract and vitreous hemorrhage (VH), seven had retinal detachment (RD), six had endophthalmitis, and two had siderosis. The median time of PPV after injury was 7.1 days. 44.8% underwent concurrent primary repair and IOFB removal, while 55.2% underwent IOFB removal at a second stage. IOFB could be removed in all patients except four due to a deep-seated location. 82.8% patients required lens removal to facilitate IOFB removal. Favorable anatomical outcome was achieved in 89.6% patients. The mean best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) (logMAR) improved significantly (P < 0.001) from preoperative 2.4 to postoperative 1.2. The interval between primary repair and PPV, baseline BCVA, preoperative VH, and postoperative macular pucker were significantly associated with final visual outcome, while preoperative RD, subretinal bleed, and endophthalmitis were not associated with final visual outcome. CONCLUSION: Although limited by a relatively small retrospective cohort, the current study showed that early PPV with appropriate adjunctive measures significantly improved anatomical and functional outcomes in most CHI-IOFB cases. RD, endophthalmitis, and siderosis were major complications associated with CHI-IOFB at presentation. Deep-seated IOFB beyond the optic nerve head or post-equatorial scleral coats posed surgical challenges in IOFB retrieval, highlighting the importance of appropriate preoperative imaging and evaluation in cases with complex posterior segment CHI-IOFB.

items.title: Cloud-deployable deep learning for smartphone-based body fluid cytology: a multi-architecture evaluation of YOLO and RT-DETR models
items.abstract: Abstract Accurate cytological evaluation of body fluid specimens is essential for diagnosing inflammatory and malignant conditions, yet manual interpretation remains labor-intensive and subject to inter-observer variability. This study developed and deployed a smartphone-based deep learning framework for multi-class body fluid cell classification integrating object detection, ROI-based classification, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Three hundred Wright–Giemsa–stained cytospin slides, one per patient, were used to generate 7149 smartphone-acquired images, which were annotated and curated into seven predominant cell classes. To reduce data leakage, images were partitioned at the source-photograph (slide-field) level. Five detection architectures (YOLOv8n, YOLOv10n, YOLOv11n, YOLOv11n-seg, and RT-DETR) were trained and evaluated on a held-out test set. YOLOv11n-seg achieved the highest mAP@50 (0.840), mAP@50–95 (0.757), and precision (0.772), while YOLOv11n achieved the highest recall (0.823). For YOLOv11n-seg, confusion-matrix macro-F1 and weighted-F1 were 0.720 and 0.730, respectively. Eosinophils, lymphocytes, and neutrophils were among the better-recognized classes, whereas errors were more frequent among monocytes, macrophages, and mesothelial cells. Grad-CAM++ analysis showed that model activation was predominantly centered within cell regions but was interpreted only as supportive model-inspection evidence. A Streamlit web application demonstrated browser-based inference with detection overlays, cell counts, differential composition, and data export. The system should currently be regarded as research, educational, and decision-support prototype rather than a standalone diagnostic device. External validation with patient-level separation, multiple imaging configurations, and broader cell populations is required before clinical application can be considered.

items.title: Code Detectors Have a Half-Life: Obsolescence and Metric Illusions in LLM-Generated Code Detection
items.abstract: Code detectors can become obsolete as code-generating models evolve: a detector validated on one generation of models may not transfer to the next. We call this limited useful life a detector half-life. We evaluate eight general-purpose LLM judges and three dedicated detectors on human-written code and code produced by seven generators across C++, Java, and Python. Our results reveal two problems. First, performance varies considerably across generators and prompting strategies, suggesting that some detectors rely on generator-specific patterns rather than general evidence of code provenance. Second, accuracy can conceal severe prediction bias. DetectCodeGPT and GPT-Sniffer achieved an accuracy of 0.50 but an F1 score of 0.00 across all generators because they classified almost every sample as AI-generated. However, general-purpose LLM judges achieved stronger accuracy and F1 scores. Our results show that general-purpose LLMs are promising training-free judges of code provenance and can outperform dedicated detectors. However, their reliability depends on the judge model, the code generator, and the prompting strategy. We therefore recommend evaluating LLM judges across multiple generators and reporting macro-F1 alongside class-specific precision and recall.

items.title: Code-MUE: Measuring Code LLMs’ Uncertainty through Execution-Based Semantic Interaction Graphs
items.abstract: As Code Large Language Models (LLMs) become central to modern software engineering, their inherent stochasticity poses significant real-world risks, where even minor errors can lead to severe functional, security, or safety consequences. Reliable automation, therefore, demands the ability to distinguish between confident, well-supported predictions and stochastic guessing. However, existing uncertainty estimation methods face a critical gap: white-box and grey-box techniques are often inapplicable to closed-source models, while standard black-box text metrics fail to capture the unique fragility of code, where syntactic variation does not necessarily imply semantic divergence. To bridge this syntax-semantics gap, we introduce Code-MUE, a purely black-box framework that measures uncertainty through execution-based Semantic Interaction Graphs. Unlike prior approaches that rely on superficial textual similarity, Code-MUE grounds uncertainty in observable runtime behavior and calculates the von Neumann entropy of the solution space to quantify global semantic diversity. A large-scale empirical study across eight state-of-the-art LLMs demonstrates that Code-MUE achieves a strong negative correlation with functional correctness, with Spearman’s correlation reaching up to −0.98. It significantly outperforms lexical and embedding-based baselines while enabling robust risk detection and selective prediction in practical workflows.
